page.title: Slack in real time
page.kicker: Lecture 04 · week 2, day 2 · running case: Slack
page.dek: Tour the non-relational database families by what each gives up, then design how Slack gets one message to everyone in a channel in real time.
page.description: Lecture 04: document, key-value, column-oriented and graph databases and when to pick SQL, then Slack's real-time chat: schema, message guarantees, scaling WebSocket servers with a real-time Pub/Sub.

chapters.title: “NoSQL” is not one thing
chapters.summary: Name the database, not the family. The two meanings of consistency, what non-relational stores give up to scale, and why relational databases scale too.

chapters.title: Documents and key-value stores
chapters.summary: Two families defined by how you may touch the data: query inside a document, or only ever get and put by key, and what each restriction buys.

chapters.title: Column-oriented databases
chapters.summary: Same table, two layouts on disk. Why an analytics query reads two files instead of every row, why warehouses compress so well, and why they are never the primary copy.

chapters.title: Graph databases
chapters.summary: The most misunderstood family. Not for anything you can draw as a graph, but for real graph algorithms: recommendations and fraud checks inside 200 ms.

chapters.title: Why they scale, and when to pick SQL
chapters.summary: No relations means no checks, so data can spread out. Every database has a backstory, and a broad rule for choosing between correctness and ingestion.

chapters.title: Slack: the problem and the schema
chapters.summary: Cut “design Slack” down to real-time text chat, then build the tables: a membership noun, direct messages as two-person channels, and a checkpoint for unread counts.

chapters.title: Sending a message: guarantees first
chapters.summary: Where messages live, and how one gets there. Send over HTTP or the open WebSocket? Three ways to persist a message, Slack, WhatsApp and Zoom, and why the edge server stays dumb.

chapters.title: Scaling WebSocket servers
chapters.summary: One channel's members land on different servers. A TCP link, then a mesh that eats each server's connections, then a real-time Pub/Sub and a balancer that keeps an organisation together.

chapters.title: The whole system
chapters.summary: One WebSocket per product, the overall architecture, what happens when a real-time message is lost, how exposed the edge servers can be, and how a write survives a dead node.

chapters.title: Deleting, ordering, and what to keep
chapters.summary: Two follow-up features answered with the same blocks: deleting a message and putting messages in order. Then the habits to keep and where this lecture stops.
